title: Generative & Agentic AI in Telecom: Shift to AI-Native Networks
summary: Generative and agentic AI are reshaping telecom networks. Learn why real-time AI systems require AI-native wireless architectures built for distributed compute, low latency, and adaptive decision-making.
body_text: Generative & Agentic AI in Telecom: Shift to AI-Native Networks Generative and agentic AI are reshaping telecom networks. Learn why real-time AI systems require AI-native wireless architectures built for distributed compute, low latency, and adaptive decision-making. July 2026 InterDigital Comms AI Generative and agentic AI systems bring together two distinct but complementary AI capabilities to telecom networks: Generative AI can help the system understand an instruction, interpret context, generate an answer, summarize information, predict an outcome, or reconstruct media. Agentic AI can decide when to use those capabilities, coordinate across tools and services, and adapt when conditions change This convergence will require wireless systems to provide the latency, reliability, compute coordination, context awareness, and safety guardrails needed for real-time intelligent action, pushing future networks toward service-aware, compute-aware, context-aware, and eventually AI-native architectures. What True Generative-Agentic AI Looks Like in Wireless Networks In wireless and telecom contexts, it is important to distinguish between using a generative model and being truly agentic . A generative foundation model alone does not make a system agentic. It must combine generative capabilities with the architecture needed to pursue a goal, maintain context, use tools, monitor results, and adapt over time. In a wireless network, being truly agentic might mean an AI system that can: Interpret network conditions Decide whether to run inference on the device, at the edge, or in the cloud Call network or compute resources through APIs Monitor whether latency or packet loss is degrading performance Adjust its plan when conditions change It is not simply generating an output; it is coordinating decisions across communication, compute, and control. Why Real-Time AI Systems Need More Than Model Intelligence Teleoperation shows why agentic AI networks need more than model intelligence. In a remote-driving scenario, a vehicle may stream live video over a cellular connection to a human operator. If that video becomes pixelated, frozen, or delayed, the operator may lose situational awareness at a safety-critical moment. In InterDigital’s AI-enabled teleoperation demo , generative and agentic capabilities work together to reduce that risk. Media delivery AI agents monitor network conditions across the vehicle and network, learn when and where video degradation is likely to occur, and adapt video encoding, bandwidth, and compute placement before quality breaks down. At the same time, a generative AI teleoperator assistant interprets live vehicle feeds and environmental data to help the operator understand hazards and make better decisions. The point is not that AI replaces the human operator. It is that AI agents can support real-time action only when generation, decision-making, network awareness, and safety are coordinated together. Teleoperation makes the broader challenge concrete: these systems need wireless networks that can help them interpret context, anticipate degradation, allocate resources, and preserve reliable service in real time. This is the central challenge of agentic AI in wireless systems: the model generates and interprets information, and the agentic layer acts on it. When that action depends on live network conditions, video quality, compute availability, and safety constraints, the limits of today’s wireless systems become clear. The Challenges of Generative-Agentic AI in Wireless Networks Generative AI and agentic AI create different risks on their own, but the convergence of the two raises the stakes in wireless systems. A generative model may interpret network context, reconstruct degraded video, predict a condition, or summarize sensor inputs. An agentic layer may then decide whether to act on that output, call a tool, shift compute resources, change compression settings, prioritize traffic, or alert a human operator. That means the core challenge is not only whether the AI model is accurate. It is whether the full generative-agentic system can produce, evaluate, and act on information quickly and safely under real wireless conditions. Latency and Timing Constraints Generative models can have variable inference times, especially when they are interpreting complex inputs, reconstructing media, or producing multimodal outputs. That variability becomes more serious when an agentic layer is waiting on the output to make a time-sensitive decision. In a traditional enterprise workflow, if an agent takes a few extra seconds to summarize a report or update a CRM, the consequence is usually a delay. In a wireless system, the same delay could mean an agent acts on stale sensor data, degraded video, or incomplete network information. For some real-time wireless control loops, responses may need to occur within a few to 10 milliseconds. In those cases, a model that occasionally takes 50 milliseconds to respond may be too slow, because the agent could act on stale sensor, video, or network information. State Consistency Across Device, Edge, and Cloud Generative-agentic systems may depend on context from multiple places at once: device sensors, edge compute, cloud models, network conditions, video feeds, and policy rules. If those sources fall out of sync, the generative layer may interpret an outdated view of the environment, and the agentic layer may act on the wrong context. This becomes especially important when AI workloads move between device, edge, and cloud. The system needs to maintain enough shared state for agents to coordinate decisions without assuming that every tier has the same real-time picture. State consistency is not only a networking problem. Agentic systems also need to preserve task context, constraints, and goals over multi-step operations. If an agent loses earlier instructions or mismanages long-horizon context, it may make locally reasonable decisions that conflict with the original service objective or safety constraints. Cascading Failures and Security Risks When generative AI and agentic AI converge, errors can propagate from interpretation to action. A generative model might reconstruct missing content incorrectly, misread a sensor pattern, or summarize network conditions inaccurately. If an agentic layer treats that output as reliable, it may trigger a sequence of decisions before the system can correct course. Greater autonomy also expands the security surface. Agentic systems may call tools, access APIs, trigger workflows, or influence network behavior. That makes prompt injection, false measurements, compromised services, or adversarial inputs more serious, because the risk is no longer only that the system generates an incorrect output; it may act on that output. New AI Traffic Patterns The convergence of generative and agentic AI also changes network traffic. A generative model may need prompts, sensor data, video frames, model updates, or multimodal inputs. An agentic layer may create bursts of traffic as it coordinates with tools, other agents, edge resources, or network functions. As a result, AI workloads may be bursty, uplink-sensitive, latency-sensitive, multimodal, and dependent on distributed compute. Some messages may be small but time-critical, while others may be large but less urgent. Service performance depends not only on radio conditions, but also on where compute is available, how quickly a model can respond, and whether the network can recognize which traffic matters most in the moment. Energy, Data, and Trust This convergence also makes deployment harder. Generative models can be compute-intensive, while agentic systems may need to run continuously, monitor conditions, and decide when to invoke heavier AI capabilities. That creates energy challenges for devices and edge infrastructure. These systems also need trustworthy data. Generative AI depends on high-quality inputs and training data, while agentic AI depends on accurate operating context before it takes action. AI-enabled wireless systems will need clearer frameworks for how data is exposed, collected, governed, and shared across the network, including who can generate data, who can access it, and under what conditions. Trust and explainability matter because these systems are not only producing outputs. They may influence decisions that affect network performance, service reliability, and safety. Operators, regulators, and users need to understand why a system acted, not just what it generated. What Wireless Networks Need to Support Generative-Agentic AI These challenges cannot be solved within AI models alone. Real-time generative-agentic systems depend on networks that can support the complexity of AI traffic, distributed compute, and time-sensitive decision-making, while also defining clear limits around what AI systems are allowed to control. Prioritize AI Traffic Based on Service Needs A small control message from an autonomous system may matter more than a larger media segment if it affects a time-sensitive decision. Service performance may depend not only on radio conditions, but also on where compute is available and how quickly a model can return a usable result. This distinction is especially important because AI workloads may not fit cleanly into traditional 5G quality-of-service models. In 5G, some services are handled as best-effort traffic, while others receive guaranteed bit rates for continuous flows. But AI traffic can be bursty: a service may need resources urgently during an inference request or control action, then need very little between bursts. If that traffic is treated like a continuously guaranteed service, the network may over-allocate radio resources that sit unused. If it is treated like ordinary best-effort traffic, the service may not receive resources quickly enough when a time-sensitive AI burst occurs. That is why service-aware networking matters. A service-aware radio access network, or service-aware RAN, understands more than traffic volume or a generic quality-of-service class. It can account for what the service is trying to accomplish and which performance characteristics matter most. Coordinate Compute Across Device, Edge, and Cloud For AI agents built around generative models, communication and computing have to be coordinated together. Future wireless systems will need to decide where AI workloads should run, how resources should be allocated during demand spikes, and how services should adapt when network conditions change. Cloud infrastructure will remain essential for AI, but cloud-only architectures are not enough for real-time wireless systems. Services such as teleoperation, robotics, and safety-critical automation may need to respond faster than a cloud round trip allows, especially when network conditions change. The answer is not to replace cloud with edge or device computing. It is to place the right intelligence at the right tier. Devices can support ultra-low-latency inference and offline resilience, but face battery, thermal, and model-size constraints. Edge systems can provide more compute close to the user, but have finite capacity. Cloud remains best for training, global optimization, analytics, and long-horizon policy updates. The architectural challenge is making these placements dynamic. As network conditions, device state, application requirements, and compute availability change, AI workloads may need to shift between device, edge, and cloud. Future systems will need to understand not only where compute exists, but whether it can meet the service’s latency, reliability, energy, and context requirements at that moment. Define Boundaries for AI-Driven Control The more a system can decide and act, the more important it becomes to define what it should and should not be allowed to control. In wireless systems, agency has to be designed with clear boundaries because AI decisions may affect network performance, service reliability, and safety. In practice, decision-making will likely remain hybrid. Learned models can support perception, prediction, pattern recognition, and adaptive planning, while deterministic rules enforce hard limits such as regulatory constraints, transmit power, interference thresholds, safety envelopes, and emergency fallback behavior. These systems will likely combine learned models with deterministic rules. AI may support perception, prediction, reconstruction, and adaptive planning, while rules and policies enforce limits around power, interference, safety, compliance, and human override. For example, an AI model may help optimize radio resource scheduling, but maximum transmit power and interference thresholds still need to be governed by enforceable controls. The hard design question is where to draw the boundaries: what should never be delegated to AI, what can be handled adaptively, and what should only be delegated under specific conditions or within defined guardrails? Preserve Safety Through Guardrails and Bounded Autonomy That boundary is essential in safety-critical systems. When one mistake can have serious consequences, AI-enabled wireless systems will need bounded autonomy: agents can operate adaptively within approved limits, while separate rules, policies, and safety mechanisms enforce the constraints that cannot be violated. These systems also need graceful degradation by design. A teleoperation or autonomous system should define in advance what it can do under full connectivity, what reduced capability looks like under partial connectivity, and when it must enter a safe state such as halt-and-hold rather than continuing to operate on incomplete information. In more complex environments, multiple specialized agents may coordinate across network monitoring, video quality, compute placement, and policy enforcement. The opportunity is not simply to add more agents, but to coordinate them around shared state, latency budgets, resource constraints, and safety boundaries. What Generative and Agentic AI Mean for the Telecom Industry AI-enabled wireless services will affect more than network architecture; they will reshape what operators, device manufacturers, and standards bodies need to support as intelligence becomes more distributed, real-time, and service-aware. Network Operators For network operators, the opportunity is not only to automate network operations or to carry more AI traffic. It is to expose differentiated network capabilities for services that depend on latency, reliability, compute coordination, and context awareness. That will make edge infrastructure, dynamic resource allocation, and service-aware network behavior increasingly important. Manufacturers AI capability may become a more prominent differentiation feature for device and chipset manufacturers. Future devices may be evaluated not only by traditional metrics such as processing power, battery life, camera quality, or connectivity, but by how much AI they can process locally, how efficiently they can run inference, and how well they can coordinate AI workloads with the network. That could also change how applications interact with device hardware. As AI capabilities move deeper into modems and chipsets, devices may need tighter interfaces between application-layer AI and lower-level communication functions. Applications may need ways to access on-device AI capabilities, while the modem may need ways to signal network conditions, resource constraints, or available AI functionality back to the application. These devices will not only be smartphones. They may include vehicles, robots, industrial sensors, XR headsets, actuators, and other connected systems, each with different requirements for compute, power, latency, mobility, and reliability. Standards Bodies For standards bodies, the challenge is interoperability. AI-enabled services cross boundaries between the device, radio network, core network, edge compute, cloud infrastructure, application layer, and data governance. Standards will need to address not only AI inside the network, but also how networks support AI applications as first-class services. The Shift Toward AI-Native Wireless Networks Today’s networks are AI-augmented: AI can be added to optimize specific functions. In a truly AI-native system, AI would be a first-class architectural element, with each layer of the stack designed around intelligent sensing, decision-making, adaptation, and control. That shift could change how wireless systems operate across the stack. For example, an AI-native network could include: AI-optimized waveforms and coding at the air interface AI-driven MAC scheduling that behaves more like an adaptive agent than a static rule table Integrated communication and compute orchestration across device, edge, and cloud Context-aware traffic handling that adapts based on what a service is trying to accomplish Traffic differentiation by purpose, so the network can treat a real-time inference request, model update, video stream, or safety-critical control signal differently, even when they move across the same infrastructure Continuous learning and self-optimization in the core network and broader system But AI-native does not mean uncontrolled autonomy. As generative and agentic AI begin to influence real-time decisions, networks will need robust safety constraints, enforceable guardrails, auditability, explainability, and human override. The industry is not there yet. The transition to AI-native systems will likely unfold over many years, with 6G expected to be the first generation in which these principles are more fully realized. InterDigital’s research is helping advance this future across the stack, from AI-assisted physical layer design and AI-driven MAC scheduling to multi-access edge computing orchestration and agentic and generative AI capabilities in core networks and services. Some of the most important progress will happen at the intersection of wireless, video, and AI, where networks become more capable of supporting AI applications as adaptive, distributed, safe, trustworthy, and explainable services. FAQ: Generative and Agentic AI in Telecom Networks Why can’t today’s networks support real-time generative and agentic AI? Today’s 5G networks can support many AI-enabled services , but they are not fully designed for AI systems that need to interpret, decide, and act in real time. Generative and agentic AI can create variable inference times, bursty traffic, shifting compute needs, and safety-sensitive decision loops that may exceed what cloud-centric or best-effort network models can reliably support. Why is edge computing important for real-time AI? Edge computing matters because some AI-enabled services cannot wait for a round trip to the cloud. Placing compute closer to the device can help reduce latency, support faster inference, and improve resilience when network conditions change, while cloud resources remain important for larger-scale training, optimization, and analytics. Why does AI-native networking matter for 6G? AI-native networking matters for 6G because 6G is expected to support more distributed, adaptive, and intelligent services than today’s networks. 6G may be the first generation wherein which AI-native principles are more fully realized, with AI becoming a first-class architectural element across sensing, decision-making, adaptation, and control. Why is service-aware networking important for 6G? Service-aware networking is important for 6G because future AI-enabled services may have very different performance requirements depending on what they are trying to accomplish. Some AI interactions may tolerate delay, while others—such as real-time control or autonomous systems—may require immediate response. Service-aware networking allows the network to prioritize traffic and allocate resources based on service intent, latency sensitivity, reliability needs, and compute availability, rather than treating all traffic the same way. How could AI-native networks create new business opportunities for telecom operators? AI-native networks could allow operators to expose differentiated capabilities beyond basic connectivity, including low-latency compute access, adaptive resource allocation, context-aware services, and AI-optimized networking. As more services depend on real-time AI behavior, operators may have opportunities to support new classes of applications and enterprise services built around reliability, distributed intelligence, and coordinated communication and compute. What role will telecom networks play in supporting autonomous systems and real-time AI? Telecom networks will increasingly act as coordination layers for real-time AI systems, helping manage communication, compute placement, latency, reliability, and context awareness across devices, edge infrastructure, and cloud resources. In autonomous or safety-critical environments, the network may help systems adapt when conditions change, preserve service quality, and support time-sensitive decision-making that cannot rely on cloud infrastructure alone. title: AppFolio Deepens Agentic AI Across Leasing, Accounting, and Resident Operations
summary: New Realm-X capabilities shift more of the portfolio’s operational work onto the platform. The new Claude connector makes its debut at Apartmentalize, June 17-19
body_text: Santa Barbara, Calif., June 16, 2026 — AppFolio (NASDAQ:APPF), the technology leader powering the future of the real estate industry, today announced an expansion of the AppFolio Performance Platform, broadening its agentic capabilities across leasing, accounting, and resident operations and extending the real performance it already delivers for residents, owners, investors, and operators alike. These innovations advance AppFolio’s vision for Real Estate Performance Management (RPM), where success is defined by the outcomes operators produce, not the tasks they automate. At the center is the Property Performance Gap: the distance between the outcomes operators want to achieve and what their current technology allows. Closing this gap requires an AI-native platform that unifies three interconnected systems of record, action, and growth into a single experience. The AppFolio Performance Platform runs leasing, maintenance, accounting, and resident operations on that foundation, so more of the portfolio’s work happens automatically and under the operator’s control. AppFolio customers can now run complex workflows directly through Anthropic’s Claude, convert more leads around the clock, close the books faster, and move residents in with less friction, all within a single platform. New innovations include: According to AppFolio’s 2026 Property Manager Benchmark Survey, operators broadly adopting AI are establishing a distinct operational advantage, expecting 31% portfolio growth in 2026 compared to just 12% for the rest of the industry. AppFolio is built for that ambition, with AI-native architecture where intelligent workflows operate within daily property management rather than alongside it. The System of Action: Realm-X Enhancements Realm-X is AppFolio’s agentic AI layer, the system of action that executes complex workflows, surfaces the right exceptions, and operates continuously across leasing, accounting, and resident operations on governed, real-time data. AppFolio is extending its leadership in agentic AI with a secure agent-to-agent connector between Realm-X and Anthropic’s Claude . Where most AI tools only surface data or answer questions, operators can use Claude to trigger and execute complex workflows under AppFolio’s native guardrails. Teams can delegate multi-step administrative tasks from any environment while maintaining accounting, financial, and compliance accuracy, with human supervision in place across agentic actions. The newly announced Accounting Performer takes on the most time-consuming back-office work so teams can focus on the decisions that drive portfolio performance. It automatically imports and codes invoices, routes them to the right approvers, and continuously closes the books by detecting mismatches and surfacing resolutions. Its budgeting produces data-driven forecasts with transparent reasoning, and reforecasts easily as conditions change. Already generally available for email and text, Leasing Performer has expanded its capabilities to include phone calls, providing rapid, multilingual responses to incoming inquiries 24/7. It answers complex questions, schedules tours, and helps renters find available units across all affiliated properties. Built natively into AppFolio rather than bolted on through a third-party integration, it operates with a real-time view of portfolio CRM data and calendars, eliminating lead-loss vulnerabilities for high-volume properties. Property managers using Leasing Performer are seeing a dramatic lift in leasing performance, including: More than 35% increase in showings booked on average Capture of up to 55% more after-hours demand that previously went unanswered Showings scheduled in an average of 2.5 minutes over the phone Resident Messenger Performer is also now generally available, providing an always-on support experience by handling inbound resident questions on demand based on the operator’s data, policies, and rules. Beta customers saw it resolve one-third of resident inquiries automatically, giving residents faster answers and teams more time for higher-value conversations. The System of Growth: Resident Onboarding and Concierge The system of growth is where AppFolio turns resident experience into long-term property performance. Satisfied residents renew, refer, and reduce the turnover costs that erode portfolio returns, making every move-in moment a performance decision. Yet property managers cite utility setup as their top move-in pain point , a first impression that puts that performance at risk before it starts. Resident Concierge removes that friction, offering incoming renters white-glove support to set up utilities, available at no cost directly within Resident Onboarding . The System of Record: Affordable Housing Enhancements The system of record is where AppFolio keeps every number, every relationship, and every transaction, and for affordable housing operators, that means compliance accuracy at every step. Affordable Housing leasing enhancements deliver a mobile-friendly application experience built to align with evolving HUD, LIHTC, and local program mandates. Operators can build tailored templates that dynamically ask the right questions based on each program’s compliance rules, whether LIHTC, Project-Based Section 8, or local programs. AppFolio groups household applications, carries demographic details directly into verification forms, and moves prospective renters from guest cards onto a centralized digital HUD waitlist. “Real performance isn’t about doing the same things faster; it’s about building for distinct outcomes,” said Kyle Triplett, Chief Product Officer at AppFolio. “That requires a fundamentally different architecture. Our unified Performance Platform is designed from the ground up to run agentic capabilities directly on governed, real-time data. It’s how leading operators scale their portfolios with confidence and drive compounding success across their residents, investors, and teams.” AppFolio is showcasing the Performance Platform at the National Apartment Association’s Apartmentalize conference, June 17-19 . Attendees can visit booths #1635 and 1535 to see live product workflows alongside demonstrations of the new Claude connector.

title: Moveworks Review 2026: Honest Pros and Cons
summary: Explore our Moveworks review covering features, pricing, pros, cons, ServiceNow acquisition, and top AI helpdesk alternatives.
body_text: Moveworks is a major enterprise AI service desk platform, especially for large organizations with complex IT and employee support needs. But after ServiceNow’s acquisition of Moveworks, teams evaluating AI helpdesk software should look closely at fit, cost, deployment complexity, Slack-native workflows, and long-term roadmap alignment. This review breaks down where Moveworks may fit, where teams may need alternatives, and how Slack-native internal support platforms like Unthread compare for IT, HR, finance, legal, and operations teams. Key Takeaways Moveworks is built for large enterprise environments, but teams should evaluate its deployment scope, implementation needs, and pricing model before choosing it for internal support ServiceNow's 2025 Moveworks acquisition creates strategic uncertainty with questions emerging about product independence and roadmap priorities for teams not already committed to the ServiceNow ecosystem Slack-native alternatives can deliver strong AI deflection with faster setup, with platforms like Unthread achieving 40% automatic ticket resolution across IT, HR, Legal, Finance, and Procurement AI model flexibility separates modern platforms from more controlled AI architectures, as some alternatives offer bring-your-own-LLM capabilities via MCP integration for data sovereignty and compliance requirements Total cost of ownership extends beyond license fees, so teams should compare implementation support, admin effort, time to value, and pricing transparency before choosing Moveworks for internal support Moveworks After the ServiceNow Acquisition The enterprise AI helpdesk market shifted in 2025 when ServiceNow announced its acquisition of Moveworks. This move consolidated two major players but left many IT and HR teams questioning whether Moveworks remains the right choice for their internal support operations. Moveworks has established itself as an enterprise AI service desk platform. However, the acquisition raises important questions about product independence, future roadmap priorities, and whether the platform's cost and complexity make sense for organizations outside large enterprise environments. Teams evaluating AI helpdesk solutions now face a critical decision point: commit to a platform undergoing major strategic shifts, or explore alternatives that may better align with modern workplace communication patterns and faster time-to-value requirements. This review examines Moveworks honestly, acknowledging where it excels while identifying limitations that may push teams toward Slack-native alternatives better suited to modern workplace communication patterns. Whether you're evaluating Moveworks for the first time or reconsidering after the acquisition, understanding the complete picture helps you make the right decision for your organization. What Is Enterprise AI Software and Why Is It Transforming IT? Enterprise AI software automates repetitive workflows that previously consumed IT, HR, and operations teams. These platforms use natural language processing and machine learning to understand employee requests, route tickets to appropriate teams, and resolve common issues without human intervention. The transformation centers on three capabilities: Intent recognition that understands what employees actually need, not just keywords they type Automated resolution that handles routine requests like password resets, access provisioning, and policy questions Intelligent routing that escalates complex issues to the right specialist immediately Moveworks positioned itself as a leader in this space by focusing on enterprise-scale deployments across IT, HR, Finance, and Workplace services. The platform connects to many enterprise systems, including ITSM tools, HRIS platforms, and identity management solutions. However, enterprise AI effectiveness varies significantly based on deployment approach. Traditional portal-based systems require employees to leave their primary work environment to submit tickets. Purpose-built AI agents that operate within Slack can reduce this friction by keeping support closer to where employees already work, converting natural conversations into structured tickets without disrupting employee workflow. For IT teams managing internal infrastructure requests, the deployment model matters as much as the AI capabilities. A platform that requires a multi-month implementation may deliver value later than one that can be configured more quickly. Moveworks vs. the Best AI Chatbot for Business Moveworks built its reputation on conversational AI that understands employee intent and automates resolution. The platform reports meaningful ticket deflection in production environments, with some deployments saving support hours quarterly. Where Moveworks performs well: Deep enterprise integrations connecting to systems including ServiceNow, Workday, Okta, and Active Directory Multi-language support for global organizations with distributed workforces Proven experience serving large enterprise customers Moveworks considerations: Overlay architecture that adds a layer on top of Slack rather than operating natively within it More involved deployment cycles for typical enterprise implementations Sales-led pricing that teams should confirm directly during evaluation The chatbot comparison becomes more nuanced when evaluating user experience. Moveworks functions as a chat overlay that employees interact with separately from their normal Slack conversations. Alternatives like Unthread's Slack Support take a fundamentally different approach: conversations in channels like #it-help automatically become trackable tickets without requiring employees to interact with a separate bot interface. This architectural difference impacts adoption rates significantly. When employees can simply post a question in their team's help channel and receive AI assistance within that same thread, friction can decrease significantly. Deep Dive: ChatGPT-like Conversational AI for Enterprise Large language models transformed what enterprise AI assistants can accomplish. Modern platforms understand context, maintain conversation history, and generate human-quality responses that address specific employee situations. Moveworks leverages LLM capabilities for intent understanding and response generation. The system analyzes incoming requests, matches them against knowledge base content, and either resolves automatically or routes to appropriate specialists with full context. Critical considerations for LLM-powered enterprise AI: Data privacy regarding where employee conversations are processed and stored Model governance controlling which AI models handle sensitive internal communications Customization depth for training on organization-specific terminology and workflows One significant limitation is that Moveworks utilizes its own proprietary AI models. For enterprises with strict data governance requirements or existing investments in Claude, GPT-4, or internal AI instances, this creates friction. In contrast, some alternative platforms offer bring-your-own-LLM capabilities via MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration, allowing organizations to connect their preferred AI models while maintaining workflow automation. This flexibility matters increasingly as enterprises develop AI governance policies requiring specific model usage for different data sensitivity levels. The self-learning knowledge base approach also differs between platforms. Some systems require manual documentation updates, while others automatically detect repeated questions and generate draft articles for team review, continuously improving deflection rates without ongoing admin overhead. The Promise of Custom AI Chatbot Development for Internal Support Generic AI assistants handle generic questions adequately. But internal support involves organization-specific policies, proprietary systems, and workflows unique to each company. Custom AI development addresses this gap. Building effective internal support AI requires: Domain-specific training on company policies, procedures, and terminology Integration depth with HRIS, identity management, and ticketing systems Privacy controls for sensitive HR requests like payroll, benefits, and employee relations Moveworks addresses customization through its Creator Studio, allowing teams to build specific use cases and workflows. The platform's enterprise integrations enable automation across systems like Workday, Okta, and Active Directory. However, customization capability means little if configuration requires specialized expertise. Many enterprise platforms demand dedicated administrators or professional services engagement for ongoing workflow adjustments. Simpler alternatives allow teams to create automations using natural language descriptions that the system converts into working workflows. For HR service desks handling sensitive employee requests, private ticketing capabilities matter significantly. Employees submitting questions about parental leave, compensation, or workplace concerns need assurance their requests remain confidential. Platforms that support private ticket creation within Slack, routing sensitive requests to DMs rather than public channels, provide this protection without forcing employees onto separate systems. Moveworks vs. a Free Chat Bot Online: What's the Real Cost of 'Free'? Free chatbot tools flood the market, tempting budget-conscious teams with no-cost entry points. The reality proves more complex when evaluating enterprise internal support requirements. Hidden costs of free solutions: Security gaps where data processing occurs on shared infrastructure without enterprise compliance certifications Feature limitations that break down at scale or when handling sensitive employee information Integration absence requiring manual workarounds that consume more time than automation saves Support void leaving teams stranded when issues arise Moveworks is generally positioned for larger enterprise evaluations with more complex implementation and procurement requirements. For mid-market teams, it is worth comparing total cost, setup time, admin resources, and pricing transparency against lighter-weight alternatives. The middle ground offers better value: platforms with transparent per-agent pricing starting at $50 to $75 monthly that include enterprise security, compliance certifications, and dedicated support. These solutions deliver 40% automatic ticket resolution comparable to enterprise platforms at a fraction of the cost. Total cost of ownership extends beyond license fees. Factor in: Implementation time and deployment planning before value realization Training investment for administrators and end users Ongoing professional services for configuration changes and workflow updates Opportunity cost of slower resolution during lengthy rollouts C3 AI Alternatives: Why Businesses Are Exploring Enterprise AI Options The enterprise AI market consolidates rapidly, with major acquisitions reshaping competitive dynamics. The Moveworks acquisition by ServiceNow exemplifies this trend, creating both opportunities and concerns for current and prospective customers. Teams explore alternatives for several reasons: Vendor lock-in concerns following acquisitions that shift product roadmaps toward parent company ecosystems Pricing transparency when sales-led enterprise quotes require additional evaluation Deployment speed requirements that may be harder to meet with lengthy implementations Slack-native workflows that may be harder to achieve with overlay architectures Post-acquisition concerns specifically affect teams not already committed to ServiceNow. Product independence, roadmap priorities, and support quality for non-ServiceNow customers all face scrutiny. AI analytics capabilities also differentiate platforms significantly. Understanding which request types consume the most agent time, where knowledge gaps cause repeated questions, and which automations deliver measurable deflection helps teams continuously improve. Real-time tracking with AI insights identifies optimization opportunities that static reporting misses. Organizations evaluating enterprise AI investments increasingly prioritize time-to-value. Platforms that can be configured more quickly allow teams to prove ROI before committing significant budget, compared to multi-month implementations requiring substantial upfront investment. Serval AI, Serval Company, Serval ITSM: Understanding the Competitive AI Landscape The AI ITSM market includes dozens of vendors with varying approaches to internal support automation. Understanding differentiation helps teams identify solutions aligned with their specific requirements. Key differentiators across AI ITSM platforms: Deployment architecture determining whether AI operates natively in Slack or requires separate interfaces Multi-department coverage supporting IT, HR, Legal, Finance, and Procurement versus IT-only focus Setup complexity ranging from professional services support to faster activation Admin overhead for ongoing workflow management and automation adjustments Moveworks is positioned for large enterprise deployments with complex system landscapes. The platform offers broad integrations for enterprise tool combinations. For teams prioritizing Slack-native operations, the competitive landscape looks different. IT service desk solutions that turn specific Slack channels into full internal help desks, with structured ticketing, routing, and workflow automation within Slack, reduce the context-switching that can affect employee adoption. Some ticket types remain visible in-channel for quick resolution. Others move to DMs or private flows for privacy. This flexibility addresses both IT requests that benefit from public visibility and HR matters requiring confidentiality, all within a single platform. The industry trend toward faster resolution with AI assistance validates the technology investment. But resolution speed depends heavily on employee willingness to use the system. Platforms requiring portal visits or separate bot interactions see lower adoption than those integrated into existing communication workflows. Beyond Basic Automation: AI Workflow Automation Tools in 2026 Simple automation handles simple tasks. Password reset links, PTO balance lookups, and policy document retrieval can be automated by most platforms. The differentiation lies in complex, multi-step workflows that span systems and require conditional logic. Advanced automation capabilities that separate platforms: Natural language workflow creation allowing admins to describe automations in plain English Multi-step approval chains routing requests through appropriate approvers based on request type and amount Conditional routing directing tickets to specialists based on content analysis and urgency Cross-system actions triggering updates in ITSM, HRIS, and identity systems from single requests Moveworks' Creator Studio provides workflow building capabilities with connections to enterprise systems. The platform handles complex automation scenarios including software provisioning, employee onboarding sequences, and IT incident response. However, automation complexity cuts both ways. Platforms requiring extensive professional services for workflow creation increase ongoing costs and slow iteration. Visual drag-and-drop automation builders combined with natural language configuration allow teams to adjust workflows as requirements change without waiting for vendor assistance. The difference in admin overhead compounds over time. Organizations with frequently changing processes, growing teams, or evolving compliance requirements benefit from platforms that non-technical administrators can configure directly. Those with stable, complex workflows may find the heavier implementation of enterprise platforms acceptable. AI deflection rates across the industry show that strong results depend on ongoing optimization, knowledge base maintenance, and workflow refinement. Simpler admin interfaces can make that ongoing improvement easier to sustain. Making the Right Choice for Your Organization Moveworks may deliver value for large enterprises with complex global requirements, existing ServiceNow investments, and budget for extended implementation timelines. The platform's scale and integration depth support its enterprise positioning. For teams outside this profile, alternatives better balance capability against cost and complexity. Employee support platforms that operate natively within Slack, offer faster setup, and use transparent per-agent pricing can provide a simpler path for internal support teams. The acquisition by ServiceNow adds another consideration. Teams committed to the ServiceNow ecosystem may find tighter integration valuable. Those seeking vendor independence face increased uncertainty about Moveworks' standalone future. Evaluate based on your specific requirements: deployment timeline, budget constraints, Slack adoption, multi-department needs, and internal technical resources for ongoing configuration. The right platform fits your organization today while scaling with your growth tomorrow. Frequently Asked Questions How does Moveworks handle sensitive HR requests differently from IT tickets? Moveworks supports separate channels for HR versus IT requests, but the underlying architecture treats both similarly as enterprise service management cases. For organizations requiring strict privacy controls where employees submit confidential requests about compensation, workplace concerns, or personal matters, purpose-built private ticketing within Slack provides stronger separation. Platforms that route sensitive requests to private DMs rather than shared channels ensure only designated HR team members see confidential submissions, with full audit trails for compliance. What happens to existing Moveworks implementations now that ServiceNow owns the company? ServiceNow has committed to maintaining Moveworks as a product while integrating its AI capabilities into the broader ServiceNow platform. Existing customers continue receiving support and updates. The strategic concern centers on long-term roadmap priorities: will non-ServiceNow integrations receive equal investment? Will pricing remain stable or migrate toward ServiceNow's enterprise model? Organizations with multi-year contracts maintain their terms, but teams evaluating new implementations should factor acquisition uncertainty into vendor selection. Can mid-market companies (500 to 2,000 employees) justify Moveworks pricing? Mid-market companies should evaluate Moveworks carefully against their budget, implementation resources, and expected support volume. Sales-led enterprise pricing and implementation requirements may fit larger organizations with complex global needs, while Slack-native alternatives with transparent per-agent pricing can be easier to model for leaner internal support teams. How do I evaluate whether my team needs enterprise-grade AI helpdesk versus simpler solutions? Consider three factors: integration complexity, deployment resources, and required customization. If you need connections across many enterprise systems with complex data flows, enterprise platforms may provide the necessary breadth. If your team lacks dedicated administrators for multi-month implementations, simpler solutions deliver faster value. If your workflows change frequently, platforms with no-code configuration reduce ongoing dependency on vendors. Most organizations overestimate their complexity requirements. Start with solutions operational within days, prove value, and migrate to enterprise platforms only if genuine limitations emerge. What specific metrics should I track to measure AI helpdesk effectiveness? Beyond basic deflection rates, track resolution time by ticket category, employee satisfaction scores per department, escalation patterns showing which request types AI handles poorly, and knowledge gap indicators revealing questions without adequate documentation. First-contact resolution rate specifically measures whether AI provides correct answers initially or requires human correction. Agent time saved translates deflection percentages into actual hours recovered. Compare these metrics monthly to identify optimization opportunities and demonstrate ROI to leadership. Platforms with built-in AI analytics automate much of this tracking, reducing manual reporting overhead.

Philtrum Length: The 2026 Ultimate Guide
summary: What's the ideal philtrum length? Learn how it's measured, why it changes with age, and how AI facial analysis reveals your own proportions.
body_text: Philtrum length is the vertical distance between the base of your nose and the peak of your upper lip's Cupid's bow. It's a small stretch of skin, but it quietly shapes how young, balanced, and expressive a face reads — and it's one of the first landmarks facial analysts, AI or human, measure when they map the lower face. What Is Philtrum Length? The philtrum is the vertical groove running from the bottom of your nose to your upper lip. Clinically, philtrum length is measured as the straight-line distance between two landmarks: subnasale (Sn) , where the columella meets the upper lip skin, and labrale superius (Ls) , the midpoint of the upper lip's vermilion border. It's a standard measurement in both aesthetic medicine and orthodontic assessment, and it's one of the eleven ratios used in classic facial-proportion analysis. What Is the Average Philtrum Length? Averages vary by sex, ethnicity, and the study cited, but most clinical literature clusters around similar bands: Population Average Philtrum Length Source Adult women (general) ~20 mm mid-philtral height Naini, 2022 Adult men (general) ~22 mm mid-philtral height Naini, 2022 Korean women (Sn–Ls) 14.3 mm Shin et al., 2014 Indonesian women (Sn–Ls) 13.86 mm (range 8.3–17.6 mm) Hasibuan et al., 2024 General adult range 12–15 mm Multiple sources The spread between these numbers comes down to where on the lip the measurement stops (some studies measure to the vermilion border, others to mid-philtral height) and which population was sampled. That's why a single "average" number is less useful than knowing the general range for your own demographic. What's Considered an Ideal or Attractive Philtrum Length? Most aesthetic guidelines put the ideal philtrum length at roughly 11–13 mm for women and 13–15 mm for men , though — as with most beauty benchmarks — this is a guideline, not a rule. A shorter philtrum tends to read as more youthful and feminine, since it keeps the upper teeth slightly visible and lets the lip sit fuller. A longer philtrum is often described as more mature or elegant, and isn't inherently less attractive; it just shifts how the lower face reads. Facial balance matters more than any single measurement. A philtrum that looks "long" on one face can look perfectly proportioned on another once you factor in chin height, lip fullness, and the nose-to-chin ratio around it. Why Does Philtrum Length Change With Age? The philtrum isn't fixed for life. It grows through adolescence, tends to stabilize in early adulthood, and then gradually lengthens again from around age 30 onward. The upper lip elongates as facial soft tissue loses collagen and elastic fibers and starts to descend under gravity, making philtrum lengthening one of the earliest visible signs of lower-face aging — often showing up before other markers like jowling or nasolabial folds. How Is Philtrum Length Measured? There are two practical approaches: Manual measurement: A clinician or aesthetic practitioner uses calipers or a ruler on a frontal photo taken in natural head position, with lips lightly together, measuring straight down from subnasale to labrale superius. AI facial ratios detection: Computer vision models automatically detect from a single photo, producing a consistent measurement without the positioning errors that can creep into a handheld ruler reading. Consistency is the main advantage AI brings here — the same face measured twice by two different people can vary by a millimeter or two depending on head tilt and lip tension, while a landmark model applies the same criteria every time. Can Philtrum Length Indicate a Medical Condition? An unusually smooth, flat philtrum is one of several facial features clinicians assess when evaluating fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in children, alongside other standardized markers, but it still needs the professionals to assess. Frequently Asked Questions What is a normal philtrum length? Most adults fall somewhere between 11 mm and 15 mm, with women trending toward the shorter end and men toward the longer end. Clinical studies report averages anywhere from about 12 mm to 22 mm depending on the exact population used. Is a short philtrum considered attractive? Generally yes, particularly in women — a shorter philtrum is associated with youth and femininity because it keeps slightly more of the upper teeth visible. That said, overall facial harmony matters more than any isolated measurement. Does philtrum length change as you age? Yes. The upper lip gradually elongates as facial soft tissue loses elasticity and descends over time, making philtrum lengthening one of the earlier visible signs of facial aging. Can philtrum length indicate a medical condition? An unusually smooth, flat philtrum is one of several facial features clinicians assess when evaluating fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in children, alongside other standardized markers. It's a professional diagnostic observation, not something to self-diagnose from a photo. How accurate is AI measurement of philtrum length compared to manual measurement? AI detection identifies the same areas used in clinical measurement, and because it applies identical criteria every time, it tends to be more consistent across repeated scans than a handheld ruler, which is more sensitive to head position and lip tension. Can I change my philtrum length without surgery? Makeup techniques like lip overlining can create the visual impression of a shorter philtrum, and dermal fillers are sometimes used to lift the Cupid's bow. Permanent changes typically require a surgical lip lift, which is a decision to make with a qualified provider, not a DIY project. Curious what your own facial proportions look like? title: Are Bounding Boxes Necessary for Object Detection?
summary: Are bounding boxes necessary for object detection? We experiment to discover whether center pointing or bounding boxes are more efficient.
body_text: One of the primary applications of computer vision is object detection, which is used to locate and count objects in images or video frames. Object detection has thousands of practical applications and is one of the most commonly used forms of computer vision. Typically, an object detector detects an object by drawing a rectangle (“bounding box”) around the object. This means that the training data also needs to be annotated with bounding boxes, which can be time consuming and tedious. This begs the question: are bounding boxes always necessary? Are there more efficient ways to do object detection? In this article, we compare two platforms that use different object detection methods to make a case for an alternative to bounding boxes — center points. When are bounding boxes unnecessary? If you want to know the rough size or extent of a detected object, you need bounding boxes. For example, if you’re detecting license plates so you can blur them, you need to know the extent of the plate. But there are many cases when bounding boxes are unnecessary: When you want to detect the count of objects in an image. For example, counting the number of homes visible in aerial photographs. When you want to determine the position of objects within the frame without needing to understand their boundaries or size. For example, detecting if your product is on the top, middle, or bottom shelf in a grocery store. When you want to detect the presence or absence of an object when the object you’re detecting is small in relation to the rest of the image. For example, Gardyn detects the presence of specific fruits in their indoor gardens. Some users would default to using image classification for this use case. However, since the fruits are very small compared to the entire image, using object detection yields better results. From our conversations with Nyckel customers, the three bullet points above cover a significant chunk of object detection use cases. Any efficiencies gained from ditching bounding boxes in favor of center points would be compelling. Bounding boxes vs. center points When an object detector uses bounding boxes, it draws rectangular boxes around each object the model detects. For training the model, annotators also need to draw boxes around the targeted objects. Annotating bounding boxes requires multiple clicks, or a click and drag, with extra attention paid to make sure the box doesn’t cover more or less than the bounds of the object. Annotation requires a lot of time and attention to detail. Fortunately, boxing is not the only way to do object detection. Pointing to an object’s center (“center detection”) is another way and requires only specifying the position of a single point. We predict that annotating training data for center detection models is significantly faster. Let’s do a quick experiment to verify that claim. Let’s experiment: annotating bounding boxes vs. center points Our hypothesis is that annotating with points is faster than bounding boxes. We tested our hypothesis by comparing two platforms that differ in this labeling procedure: Vertex AI , which uses bounding boxes, and Nyckel , which uses center points. We measured the time it took to correctly annotate the same 50 images on each platform. Note: While we have a clear bias toward Nyckel’s product, we used a contractor who isn’t as familiar with our product as our internal team to conduct this experiment. To exclude one-time learning costs from the experiment, we asked him to familiarize himself with both products before conducting the experiment. The input data Roboflow has a set of 100 benchmarking datasets, called Roboflow 100 , available for this kind of experiment. We used their grass weeds data and selected 50 images at random from the dataset. Each image contained anywhere from one to 24 weeds. These are the kind of images included in the dataset: Sample images from the Roboflow 100 dataset Our experience annotating with Vertex AI’s bounding boxes When using Vertex AI, placing boxes near the edge of the frame sometimes resulted in misfires, adding a second or two each time. This was particularly a problem on the left margin because the UI only likes users to drag a rectangle from left to right. Also, correctly getting the minimal bounding box that includes a whole object doesn’t always work on the first try. User draws bounding boxes to annotate data for object detector Our experience annotating with Nyckel’s center points As you will see in the results below, annotating points was significantly faster. In addition, a noticeable difference with Nyckel is that Nyckel trains the model while you annotate, showing its predictions on training images after you’ve annotated just a handful of them. These model predictions are startlingly accurate, and they guide the eye in annotating subsequent images. However, the suggested annotations occasionally include false positives and sometimes fail to identify borderline object cases, meaning that Nyckel’s suggestions need to be verified by a human eye during the annotating process. User annotates data using center points for object detector The results The difference is pretty striking between the two methods of object annotation: a factor of 3 difference! The additional clicks and image inspection time for the bounded box method quickly add up. If your use case doesn’t need bounding boxes, platforms using center-point detection have a clear advantage in annotation time and tedium. What about model accuracy? So, how do the models generated by Nyckel and Vertex AI compare for this data? Great question! Stay tuned; we’ll be answering that question soon through a benchmark of the performance of different object detection products. In the meantime, you can try us out or read about how Gardyn picked us over Azure because of better model accuracy. Conclusion: Bounding boxes vs. center points Annotating center points is 3x less time-consuming than annotating bounding boxes. If you only need to detect the presence, number, and/or relative positions of objects, you are working too hard if you are using bounding boxes. ____ Thinking about deploying object detection? Humidity: The Hidden Key to Energy-Efficient Homes As homes grow tighter and more efficient than in previous generations, managing indoor humidity is critical to comfort, HVAC performance, and overall home comfort Air Comfort Energy Pro 4/27/26 By: Dan Bereiter, Senior Product Manager, Resideo Homeowners looking to improve energy efficiency can invest in the best insulation, windows, and HVAC systems available, but they may still feel uncomfortable. The missing link in many high-performance homes isn’t temperature control – it’s humidity. Humidity plays a critical role in determining how comfortable a space feels and how efficiently its systems operate. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recommends maintaining indoor relative humidity between 30% and 50%. High humidity keeps the air moist and increases the likelihood of mold. As builders continue to push for higher performance standards than in the past, homes are increasingly being built and upgraded with tighter building envelopes. The EPA notes that weatherization measures – such as sealing air leaks and adding insulation – are used to reduce uncontrolled air exchange between indoors and outdoors. That shift can help improve efficiency, but it can also change how indoor environments behave. Additionally, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) notes that in hot and humid climates, indoor spaces are not comfortable unless both temperature and humidity are properly controlled; without proper humidity management, even a well-designed HVAC system may struggle to deliver the comfort homeowners expect. This shift is reshaping how builders and HVAC professionals think about high-performance homes. As humidity moves to the forefront of home performance, new solutions are redefining how it’s managed. The challenge of tighter, modern homes To understand why humidity matters more today compared to older, naturally ventilated homes, it helps to look at how homes themselves are changing. Modern construction techniques prioritize airtight building envelopes to reduce energy loss. According to the DOE, reducing the amount of air that leaks in and out of the home is a cost-effective way to cut heating and cooling costs and increase comfort. At the same time, everyday activities, from cooking and showering to doing laundry, continue to introduce moisture indoors. In a tightly sealed home, that moisture has limited pathways to escape and can accumulate over time. The EPA states that weatherization can reduce the exchange of indoor and outdoor air, and that pollutants can build up indoors if not properly managed. Temperature alone is no longer a reliable indicator of comfort either. An HVAC system may reach the thermostat setpoint, but homeowners may still feel uncomfortable because humidity, airflow, ventilation, and filtration all interact to shape the indoor environment. As many contractors have experienced firsthand, the thermostat can say everything is fine while the homeowner is still uncomfortable. In many cases, the missing variable is humidity. How balanced humidity impacts comfort and efficiency Humidity directly influences how people perceive temperature. In the summer, excess humidity can make a room feel warmer than it is, leading homeowners to lower the thermostat and increase cooling demand. In the winter, overly dry air can create discomfort that prompts occupants to raise the heat. From an HVAC system perspective, moisture also represents a significant portion of the cooling workload. The EPA notes that in humid climates, air conditioners must both cool the air and remove moisture to maintain comfort; otherwise, the air will feel uncomfortably damp even if the temperature is cool. When humidity is not properly managed, HVAC systems must work harder than necessary to maintain comfort. Balanced humidity also protects building materials and supports cleaner indoor environments. For example, the EPA notes that excess moisture may lead to mold growth and damage to building materials. For this reason, humidity management is increasingly considered a core component of whole-home performance. Backed by 150,000 hours of runtime and ENERGY STAR® certified performance, the Honeywell Home Whole Home Dehumidifier is a reliable solution that helps maintain optimal comfort and energy efficiency across a variety of home environments. Humidity control in the future of high-performance homes As residential construction continues to evolve, builders and contractors are increasingly designing homes around the concept of complete indoor environmental control. Temperature, humidity, ventilation, and filtration are becoming interconnected parts of a broad indoor environmental system, and advances in sensing technology and connected devices are helping make this system-level approach practical. Modern HVAC equipment and IAQ solutions are incorporating additional sensors and clear, actionable diagnostics, allowing professionals to identify performance trends and address issues early. Rather than relying solely on reactive service calls, the industry is moving toward more proactive management of indoor environments. This shift reflects an ongoing trend in HVAC: comfort and air quality are becoming measurable system outcomes, not just subjective homeowner experiences. Energy efficiency is no longer just about how well a home holds conditioned air; it is about how effectively the entire indoor environment is balanced. Treating humidity as a core part of home performance allows builders, contractors, and homeowners to create indoor environments that feel more comfortable, operate efficiently, and support long-term durability. Why can modern homes have more humidity problems than older homes? Energy-efficient homes are designed with tighter insulation, air sealing, and high-performance windows to help reduce energy loss. body_text: Most businesses can only imagine the kind of sustained robust growth achieved by Schweiger. But as a company grows, so do the complexities and challenges of revenue cycle management (RCM). For Schweiger, a decentralized RCM function proved to be inadequate as the group entered its phase of rapid expansion. Notably, the organization struggled to manage a sizable array of payer contracts—more than 200 and growing. “In particular, we found it difficult to model out these contracts and determine whether we were receiving the full, appropriate reimbursement,” explains Yta Toribio, Schweiger’s Sr. Vice President of Revenue Cycle Management. “We saw a lot of revenue leakage as a result.” Further compounding this challenge, she adds, Schweiger lacked an in-house analytics team that could process complex RCM data. “In the absence of this internal capability, we needed a data and analytics solution without a steep learning curve—and we needed it fast.”

body_text: Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is a thermoplastic elastomer used in wheels, seals, footwear parts, cable jackets, films, hoses, and molded industrial components. Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) combines plastic melt processability with rubber-like elasticity, giving the material flexibility, rebound behavior, abrasion resistance, and shape recovery after repeated deformation. TPU belongs to the polyurethane family and contains hard segments that support strength, plus soft segments that support elasticity. Grade chemistry controls hardness, oil resistance, hydrolysis resistance, and low-temperature flexibility. Covestro lists Desmopan and Texin TPU grades across 60 to 98 Shore A and 30 to 75 Shore D hardness ranges. TPU production uses injection molding, extrusion, blow molding, film casting, coating, calendaring, and additive manufacturing, depending on the target part geometry. Thermoplastic behavior lets TPU soften during heating, flow into a mold or die, then harden again after cooling, which separates it from crosslinked rubber. Industrial relevance comes from balanced toughness, tear resistance, wear resistance, chemical resistance, and flexible performance under repeated movement. TPU appears in automotive interiors, medical tubing, sports equipment, electronics protection, conveyor belts, gaskets, and precision parts where flexible durability matters. Material selection depends on the hardness target, service temperature, contact fluids, part thickness, and processing route for the finished component. What Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU)? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is a melt-processible thermoplastic elastomer that combines plastic processing behavior with rubber-like flexibility. TPU belongs to Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE), a material group that delivers thermoplastic behavior and elastomeric properties in one polymer family. TWI defines Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE) as copolymers or compounds with thermoplastic and elastomeric properties. TPU works as an engineering plastic because it provides abrasion resistance, tear strength, oil resistance, grease resistance, flexibility, and durable mechanical performance. SpecialChem describes TPU as a melt-processable thermoplastic elastomer with high durability and flexibility. Hard and soft polymer segments give TPU its hybrid structure, where rigid segments support strength and soft segments support elasticity. TPU suits injection molding, extrusion, films, coatings, and 3D printing for parts that require flexible strength under repeated use. What Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Material Made of? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is synthesized from three primary raw materials a polyol soft segment, a diisocyanate hard segment, and a short-chain diol or diamine chain extender. Polyols come from polyester or polyether sources, and diisocyanates are commonly MDI, methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, or aliphatic diisocyanates (such as hexamethylene diisocyanate). The soft segments provide flexibility and low-temperature performance, contributing to elastic recovery and elongation at break. The hard segments form rigid, hydrogen-bonded domains that deliver tensile strength and dimensional stability. The ratio of soft to hard segments directly controls the final Shore hardness, ranging from Shore A 60 to Shore D 80, depending on formulation. Polyester-based TPU gives stronger abrasion resistance and oil resistance for mechanical parts. Polyether-based TPU gives better hydrolysis resistance and low-temperature flexibility for wet or outdoor service conditions. Chain extenders adjust molecular weight, hard segment spacing, and final mechanical performance across TPU grades. What Is the full form of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU)? "Thermoplastic Polyurethane" is the full form of the acronym "TPU," where each word describes a defining chemical or physical characteristic of the material. "Thermoplastic" indicates the material softens reversibly upon heating, and "polyurethane" identifies the urethane linkage, NHCOO, backbone formed during polymerization. TPU is categorized as a thermoplastic elastomer because it combines the melt processability of thermoplastics with the elastic deformation behavior of vulcanized rubber, without requiring irreversible crosslinking. The material returns to its original shape after deformation, a defining trait of the thermoplastic elastomer classification. Reversible softening allows TPU to be injection molded, extruded, and reprocessed under controlled heating conditions. Polyurethane chemistry gives TPU strong abrasion resistance, tear strength, and bonding ability across films, coatings, and molded parts. The acronym TPU directly reflects the material's dual identity as a heat-processable polymer and an elastic engineering material.

title: Visa Research: The Great Wealth Transfer Is Already Reshaping How Americans Spend
summary: Visa Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) estimates $36 trillion will transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years, with much of the impact already visible in housing, travel and major purchases After accounting for liabilities, removing the top 1 percent of households and subtracting
body_text: Visa Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) estimates $36 trillion will transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years, with much of the impact already visible in housing, travel and major purchases After accounting for liabilities, removing the top 1 percent of households and subtracting retirement spending, taxes and fees, approximately $36 trillion of boomers’ $93 trillion in assets will transfer to heirs over the next 20 years Nearly 75 percent of inheritance recipients already have a higher net worth, meaning most transferred wealth is likely to be saved or invested rather than spent The $8 trillion expected to be spent creates a targeted lift concentrated mostly in autos, housing, travel and retail The transfer is underway: one in four millennial homeowners received parental down payment assistance, and skip-generation travel is rising as boomers increasingly choose to share their wealth earlier SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 8, 2026-- New research from Visa Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) finds that the great wealth transfer is already influencing major financial decisions, from home purchases to travel and long-term saving. The research estimates that approximately $36 trillion will transfer from baby boomers to Gen X and millennial households over the next 20 years. The findings also show that most of this wealth will flow to households that are already financially secure, making the spending impact more targeted than transformational. “For businesses in big-ticket sectors like housing and travel, this is not a future trend to watch,” said Wayne Best, chief economist at Visa. “It is already influencing consumer decisions—and shaping where growth will be distributed in the years ahead.” The transfer is large, but more concentrated than it appears Baby boomers hold at least $93 trillion in assets, more than three times U.S. GDP. However, VBEI finds that the amount that reaches heirs is reduced significantly once you factor in debt, retirement spending, taxes, and the wealth held at the very top. The result: approximately $36 trillion transferring to Gen X and millennial households over the next 20 years, equivalent to roughly $515,000 per inheriting household. Most transferred wealth will be saved or invested Nearly 75 percent of those receiving an inheritance already have a higher net worth than the median household.1 As a result, $28 trillion of the $36 trillion is likely to be saved or invested. This dynamic represents a significant opportunity for banks, wealth managers, and fintech firms competing for assets from newly inheriting households over the next two decades. The spending lift is real but targeted to specific categories The impact will likely show up most in the areas where consumers are already making major financial decisions. Spending on autos is expected to see a 6.4 percent average annual lift over the next 20 years.2 Overall, the $8 trillion expected to flow into consumer spending will lift annual real spending growth by approximately 0.1 percentage point per year through 2046, a modest boost rather than a major shift in the economy.3 Families are choosing to share wealth earlier More families are transferring wealth earlier while they can see its impact. One in four millennial homeowners received parental down payment assistance, and 26 percent reported they would not have been able to purchase their current home without it. More than half of individuals expecting to receive an inheritance cite it as critical to their ability to purchase a home, a figure that rises to 69 percent among millennials. In travel, 28 percent of grandparents have already taken a skip-generation trip with their grandchildren, without the children’s parents, and 35 percent plan to do so within the next three years. 66 percent of boomers say they want to enjoy their wealth or have heirs enjoy it while they are alive, compared to 34 percent who plan to preserve it for after death.4 What this means for consumers and businesses For consumers, family financial support may help younger households buy homes, travel and reach major milestones sooner For businesses, the opportunity will be focused in sectors where inherited wealth is already driving major purchases, especially housing, autos, travel, retail and financial services For financial institutions, inherited wealth creates an opportunity to support households as they save, invest or purchase property The full report is available at https://usa.visa.com/partner-with-us/visa-consulting-analytics/economic-insights/great-wealth-transfer-reality-check.html Methodology VBEI’s analysis is based on internal economic modeling, data from the Federal Reserve Board, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the U.S. Department of Labor, as well as third-party consumer survey research. FAQ How large is the great wealth transfer? Visa Business and Economic Insights estimates that about $36 trillion will transfer from baby boomers to Gen X and millennial households over the next 20 years, after accounting for debt, retirement spending, taxes and other factors. How much of that wealth will actually be spent? Only a portion—about $8 trillion—is expected to translate into consumer spending, as most recipients are already financially secure and more likely to save or invest what they receive.5 Where will the spending impact be most visible? The impact is expected to be concentrated in housing, autos, travel and retail, where consumers are already making major financial decisions. Is this a future trend, or is it happening now? The transfer is already underway, showing up in real-time decisions like down payment assistance for homebuyers and increased multigenerational travel, as more families choose to share wealth earlier. About Visa Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) Visa Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) provides data-driven analysis of global economic trends, consumer spending patterns and the evolution of digital commerce, drawing on proprietary VisaNet transaction data, economic modeling and third-party research.
